newsitem.title: DUBAI: U.S. embassy in Saudi issues security advisory.
newsitem.headline: U.S. embassy in Saudi issues security advisory.

text.p: The U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia has advised Americans living in the kingdom to "exercise extreme caution" against possible attacks coinciding with Tuesday's U.S. presidential elections.

The advice, issued on an embassy emergency telephone line on Monday, said "terrorist groups" could be encouraged to attack U.S. interests and facilities because of "elections in the United States, upcoming international conferences as well as the one-year anniversary of the bombing...in Riyadh".
"This could provide an excuse for terrorist groups to attack U.S. interests or facilities over the next seven to 10 days," it added.
Five Americans and two Indians died in the blast which rocked a U.S.-run military training centre in the Saudi capital on November 13, 1995.
Four Saudis who confessed on state-run television to their roles in the blast were executed in May.

"The embassy urges all Americans throughout Saudi Arabia to exercise extreme caution and vigilance...(they) should keep a low profile, reduce travel within the country and treat mail received from unfamiliar sources with suspicion.

"The embassy and Saudi security will continue to work closely to enhance the safety of Americans. You should report any suspicious or unusual activities or incidents to the embassy or the nearest U.S. consulate," added the advisory.
There are about 35,000 Americans living in Saudi Arabia.
United States and Western troops deployed in the Gulf have stepped up security after a June 25 truck bombing in eastern Saudi Arabia that killed 19 U.S. airmen.
U.S. Defence Secretary Willian Perry said on Friday Washington had not yet determined who was behind the blast on the Khobar Towers housing complex in Dhahran.
The Washington Post reported last week that Saudi authorities had arrested 40 people in connection with the blast and were convinced that Iran backed a broad conspiracy in the attack.
Iran rejected the charges as "a new U.S. conspiracy to create internal conflict in Islamic-Arabic countries".

Perry refused to discuss details of the investigation into the truck bombing being conducted by Saudis and U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation. But he said he made clear to Saudi officials that they must cooperate fully.
Saudi officials have said they would release full details once the investigation was over.
